title: Should employers see your social media?

turns.speaker: Ray
turns.text: The recruiter admitted they search every shortlisted candidate. Not the professional profile. Everything.

turns.speaker: Stefan
turns.text: Which is legal almost everywhere, and that surprises people more than it should.

turns.speaker: Dina
turns.text: The defence is that it's public. Which is true and completely beside the point.

turns.speaker: Dina
turns.text: Public to your friends isn't public to a hiring committee. Something posted at nineteen to forty people is being read at thirty-two by a stranger deciding your income.

turns.speaker: Stefan
turns.text: Context collapse. It's the thing these platforms are worst at.

turns.speaker: Ray
turns.text: The practical problem is that you can't prove it happened. Nobody writes down that they didn't like your holiday photographs.

turns.speaker: Stefan
turns.text: Which makes discrimination law almost useless here. You learn things you're not allowed to ask about in an interview, and then you can't unknow them.

turns.speaker: Dina
turns.text: Religion, pregnancy, health, politics. All illegal to ask, all visible in ten minutes.

turns.speaker: Ray
turns.text: Germany drafted something limiting it to professional networks only, didn't they.

turns.speaker: Stefan
turns.text: They did, and enforcement is the obvious weakness. You can't police curiosity.

turns.speaker: Dina
turns.text: You can make the search a documented stage, though. Recorded, disclosed, same for every candidate.

turns.speaker: Ray
turns.text: Which most recruiters would hate, and that tells you it would work.

points: Recruiters commonly search all social media of shortlisted candidates, which is broadly legal.
Dina argues the public nature of posts is beside the point, because content shared with friends at nineteen is later read by strangers deciding employment.
Stefan identifies context collapse as the underlying problem.
Discrimination law is ineffective here because the influence cannot be proven and information cannot be unlearned.
Characteristics illegal to ask about, such as religion, pregnancy, health and politics, are visible within minutes.
Germany has drafted limits to professional networks, though enforcement is weak; Dina proposes making searches a documented, disclosed and uniform stage.
